Inhibition of the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway extends life span in all species studied to date, and in mice delays the onset of age-related diseases and comorbidities. However, it is unknown if mTOR inhibition affects aging or its consequences in humans.
These efforts are in part capitalizing on the outcomes from geroscience in model organisms over the last three decades. This study presents a limited trial with the mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) inhibitor RAD001—a molecule similar to rapamycin that also decreases mTOR activity.
RAD001 also reduced the percentage of CD4 and CD8 T lymphocytes expressing the programmed death-1 (PD-1) receptor, which inhibits T cell signaling and is more highly expressed with age. These results raise the possibility that mTOR inhibition may have beneficial effects on immunosenescence in the elderly.
